Training jobs queue behind inference, nightly batch work slips into business hours, and the on-call rotation has absorbed two pages for jobs that timed out waiting for a free card. The obvious question on the table is whether we buy more hardware or squeeze more out of what we own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the framing matters more than the arithmetic.

If a data scientist spends forty minutes a day babysitting a job scheduler, that's salary we're burning on something a machine could absorb.

But before we spend, I think we owe ourselves an honest accounting of utilisation, and what I've seen in the metrics makes me hesitant. Our aggregate GPU-hours look fully allocated, but that number is misleading. Jobs are scheduled in coarse blocks, so a task needing twenty minutes often holds a card for an hour. Memory fragmentation forces us to run smaller models than the hardware supports. Inference and training compete for the same pool with no priority tiers, so a low-stakes experiment can delay a customer-facing workload. My rough estimate is that effective utilisation sits somewhere between 45 and 60 percent of theoretical capacity. If that's even half right, we effectively own one and a half idle GPUs already. Buying more hardware before fixing that is like hiring a second cook because the first one keeps losing their knife.

There's also the question of what the money buys elsewhere. The capital we'd spend on new cards is roughly a quarter of our annual infrastructure budget. That same money could fund the observability work we've deferred, a second region for failover, or simply extend our runway. Opportunity cost is invisible when we decline to spend, but it's real, and right now the deferred reliability work is arguably a bigger risk to the product than slow training jobs.

Latency cuts both ways here, and I want to be careful not to oversell the software path. Better scheduling reduces queue latency, but it does nothing for per-token inference speed, and if our product roadmap leans harder on real-time inference, hardware headroom eventually becomes non-negotiable. The honest position is that utilisation work buys us time and clarity, not a permanent solution.

On reliability, buying more cards of the same type actually concentrates our risk: same firmware, same failure modes, same supply chain. Diversifying would help, but heterogeneous fleets raise operational complexity we're not staffed to handle. Meanwhile, the utilisation work — better queueing, priority classes, right-sized job blocks, memory-aware packing — is low-risk and independently valuable. Even if we buy hardware in six months, none of that work is wasted.

That points to reversibility as the deciding factor for me. Buying hardware is a one-way door in practice: capital committed, depreciation started, colo space consumed. Utilisation improvements are a series of small, reversible bets. **To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on our inference capacity decision

The obvious question on the table is whether we should purchase additional hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the framing matters more than the spreadsheet.

**The case for buying**

The straightforward argument for new hardware is that our utilisation is already high. When a cluster runs above roughly eighty percent sustained utilisation, queueing delays grow non-linearly — small bursts in demand produce disproportionate latency spikes. That matches what we observe: median inference latency is fine, but p95 latency degrades badly during the afternoon window, and that tail latency is exactly what our interactive users and our internal tooling feel. Buying capacity restores headroom immediately, and headroom is what absorbs the unpredictable.

There's also a reliability dimension. Right now, a single node failure during a peak period means degraded service for hours, because we have no slack to reroute work. Redundancy isn't glamorous, but it's the difference between an incident and an inconvenience.

**The case for improving utilisation**

That said, I don't think the case for buying is as clean as it first appears. When we instrumented the cluster properly last month, we found that a meaningful fraction of our "full" capacity is consumed by work that doesn't need it: batch jobs scheduled at peak hours out of habit rather than necessity, models held resident in memory that are used a few times a week, and inference requests that could be batched more aggressively with modest latency tolerance. Some of this is fixable with scheduling policy and better queueing discipline — work that costs engineering weeks, not capital.

There's also an opportunity cost argument that cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about it. Every week an engineer spends on scheduler improvements is a week not spent on product work. But every dollar spent on hardware we only partially use is a dollar not spent on those same engineers, on tooling, or held in reserve for the moment we actually need it. Hardware depreciates whether we use it well or badly; the question is which investment compounds. Better utilisation practices compound — the discipline of measuring, scheduling, and right-sizing transfers to whatever hardware we own, now or later.

This is the factor I keep returning to. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible decision. Once purchased, the capital is committed, the depreciation clock starts, and if our demand forecast is wrong — in either direction — we live with it. Improving utilisation is reversible and incremental. If a scheduling change makes latency worse, we roll it back in an afternoon. If our demand grows faster than expected, we can still buy hardware later, having learned precisely how much we need. The asymmetry favours acting on the reversible option first, especially given genuine uncertainty in our demand forecast. Our growth projections have been wrong twice in the last year, once in each direction.

**Uncertainty**

I want to acknowledge what we don't know. We don't have a full quarter of clean utilisation data post-instrumentation, so our estimate of recoverable capacity is rough. We don't know whether the demand growth we're seeing is a trend or a spike tied to a couple of internal projects that may wind down. And model efficiency improvements — quantisation, better serving stacks — keep moving the goalposts on how much hardware a given workload needs. Any of these could change the calculus.

My recommendation is a sequenced one, though not a compromise: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation work — rescheduling batch jobs off-peak, aggressive batching for latency-tolerant traffic, and unloading rarely-used models — with explicit, pre-agreed latency targets. If we hit those targets, we've deferred a significant capital purchase and learned something durable. If we miss them, we will have generated the precise data needed to size a hardware purchase correctly, and I'd support making it quickly and without further debate. Either way, we end up in a better position than buying now on an imperfect forecast. The worst outcome would be buying hardware to relieve pressure we haven't yet tried to manage, and never learning where our real ceiling is.

**Re:** Hardware investment decision for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of our existing fleet before committing to any new hardware purchase, while reserving a modest budget line for a small, targeted expansion if utilisation work stalls or demand grows faster than we can absorb. This is not a compromise for its own sake; it reflects the specific economics of our situation, where the cheapest capacity we can acquire is capacity we already own but are not using.

**Where we stand**

Our current cluster runs at roughly 40–45% average utilisation, with sharp peaks around batch inference windows and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. At the same time, we are queuing experiments and occasionally renting cloud capacity at spot prices to cover overflow. This combination — idle owned hardware alongside paid-for rented hardware — is the clearest possible signal that our problem is scheduling and orchestration, not raw capacity. Every hour a local GPU sits idle while we pay an external provider for the same class of compute is pure waste, and it is waste we control.

**Cost**

The capital cost of new hardware is only the visible part. Fully loaded, a new node brings colocation or power costs, maintenance time from a team that is already stretched, and the operational burden of keeping more machines patched, monitored, and cooled. Against that, the utilisation path costs mostly engineering time: better job scheduling, a proper queue with priorities, checkpointing so long jobs can be preempted, and time-slicing for interactive workloads. None of this is glamorous, but it is work we would need to do anyway even after buying more hardware, because poor utilisation does not fix itself with scale — it compounds. Buying more nodes before fixing scheduling means buying more idle hours.

**Latency**

The honest counterargument is latency. Interactive and latency-sensitive workloads suffer when they compete with batch jobs for the same cards, and right now our answer to that contention is avoidance: people simply don't submit work when the cluster is busy, which is one reason utilisation looks low. If we solve contention properly — with preemption, partitioning, and clear service classes — we can raise utilisation without degrading interactive performance. If we cannot, then and only then does dedicated hardware for latency-critical paths become defensible. That is the shape of the targeted expansion we would hold in reserve: not a general capacity increase, but a small dedicated pool for interactive work if the software fix proves insufficient.

**Reliability**

More hardware does improve redundancy, and our fleet is old enough that a single node failure during a peak window is a real risk. But reliability is better bought with good checkpointing and failover than with spare capacity sitting mostly unused. If a job can resume within minutes on another node, a single failure is an inconvenience; without checkpointing, it is a lost day regardless of how many spare cards we own. The utilisation workstream therefore doubles as reliability work, which strengthens the case for doing it first.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

These considerations cut both ways, and we want to be explicit about that. The engineering time spent on scheduling is time not spent on product work, and if our workload is about to grow sharply — a plausible scenario given the roadmap — we will end up buying hardware eventually anyway, and some scheduling work will have been spent on a problem that growth would have made moot. Conversely, hardware is the more reversible purchase in one sense: it can be resold or repurposed, while engineering time is gone forever once spent. But hardware purchases also commit us to power, space, and maintenance for years, and in a field where accelerator generations turn over quickly, that commitment is less reversible than it appears. On balance, we judge the scheduling investment to be the more recoverable bet: the skills and tooling transfer to any future fleet, whatever its size.

**Uncertainty**

Our demand forecast is the largest unknown. If the next quarter brings a step change in workload — a new product surface, a large customer, a research push — the utilisation ceiling will arrive quickly and we should not have delayed purchasing. We will return in six weeks with utilisation figures, queue latency data, and a revised recommendation.

Inference traffic has grown roughly 40% over the past two quarters, and our batch training windows are increasingly squeezed into nights and weekends. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional hardware or invest in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own. **The case for buying**

The straightforward argument for new hardware is that it removes the constraint immediately. Our queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and that latency is not cosmetic — it shows up in product experience and in developer productivity, since our internal tooling shares the same fleet. Every hour a researcher waits for a job to schedule is an hour of expensive human time idling, and that opportunity cost is real even if it never appears on a hardware invoice. Buying also has a reliability benefit we should not dismiss: a larger fleet gives us headroom for failover, maintenance windows, and the kind of experimental workloads that currently get deprioritised because they might destabilise production serving.

**The case against buying first**

But the purchase path has costs that are easy to underestimate. Capital hardware depreciates quickly in a market where model architectures and accelerator generations turn over every eighteen months or so. A purchase made today to solve a peak-hour problem locks us into capacity that sits idle off-peak — our current fleet averages well under 40% utilisation across a full day, even while individual peak hours run hot. Paying to add capacity at the bottom of that curve is the expensive way to solve a peak problem. There is also an opportunity cost in engineering attention: procurement, racking, and integrating new machines would consume weeks of the same people we would ask to do the optimisation work. If our traffic growth softens, or if a model change halves our serving cost, we carry the excess.

Improving utilisation, by contrast, is cheap, fast, and reversible. Most of the candidate work — better batching of inference requests, smarter scheduling that lets short jobs fill gaps between long training runs, quantisation of our two largest serving models, and killing a handful of zombie workloads that reserve GPUs they rarely use — can be shipped incrementally and rolled back if it misbehaves. We estimate this work could defer a purchase by two to three quarters, which at our scale is a meaningful amount of capital retained and a meaningful reduction in the risk of buying at the wrong size.

**Reliability and latency caveats**

We want to be honest about the trade-off. Utilisation gains of this kind tend to raise average load, which can increase tail latency if we push too far. We will therefore treat p99 serving latency as a hard guardrail: if optimisation work drives tail latency beyond our agreed threshold, we stop optimising and trigger the purchase path. Similarly, we will not trade away redundancy — the scheduling improvements must preserve our ability to lose a machine without degrading production service. Reliability is not a line item we are willing to spend to save money.

Our recommendation: fund a focused six-week utilisation effort now, with a pre-approved hardware purchase as the explicit fallback if we miss the utilisation or latency targets. New hardware is not just the sticker price. Meanwhile, the utilisation numbers suggest we could recover the equivalent of two to three GPUs' worth of capacity through software and process changes alone, at a cost of perhaps a few engineer-weeks. If our problem were uniformly high demand, buying more hardware would be the obvious answer. Instead, our problem is concentrated demand, and concentrated demand is a scheduling problem before it is a procurement problem.

The cost asymmetry reinforces this. New hardware at the tier we'd want would run to a seven-figure capital outlay, plus the ongoing costs of power, cooling, rack space, and the operational burden of managing a larger fleet. Improving utilisation, by contrast, means engineering time: building a proper job queue, enabling batched inference where latency budgets allow, quantising models so more requests fit per card, and shifting batch workloads like fine-tuning and evaluation runs into off-peak windows. That's perhaps two engineers for a quarter — real money, but an order of magnitude less than the hardware path, and it's an expense we already have headcount to absorb.

Batching and queueing trade throughput for response time, and some of our interactive features have tight latency budgets that batching could violate. But the right response to that tension is not to buy hardware preemptively; it's to segment our workloads deliberately. Interactive traffic gets dedicated capacity and priority scheduling, while batch work fills the gaps. Reliability cuts both ways. More machines mean more redundancy, and a single failed card today can genuinely hurt us during peak hours. But our current reliability incidents have mostly stemmed from configuration drift and ad hoc job placement, not from raw hardware scarcity. Better orchestration improves reliability too — automatic failover between cards, health checks, and the ability to drain a machine for maintenance without dropping traffic. Buying hardware without fixing our operational practices would just give us more ways to misconfigure things.

Then there is opportunity cost and reversibility, which I think are the most underweighted factors in this debate. Capital spent on GPUs is largely sunk; hardware depreciates quickly, and the market moves fast enough that a purchase made today may look poorly matched to next year's model landscape. Engineering effort spent on scheduling, batching, and observability is portable — it makes any future fleet, whether owned or rented, run better, and the skills and tooling transfer directly. If we later do buy hardware, we'll buy less of it because we'll know exactly what our true peak demand is. Conversely, if demand shifts toward cloud providers or toward smaller, more efficient models, the utilisation work loses little value while a hardware purchase loses a great deal.

We should, however, place a conditional order or at minimum secure vendor pricing now, so that if the utilisation work underdelivers we can execute a purchase without paying the lead-time penalty in reliability or latency.

**The case for buying**

The simplest argument for new hardware is that demand is real and growing. Our p95 inference latency has crept from 180ms to 310ms over six months, and we have begun queueing batch jobs behind interactive traffic. Every point of latency degradation carries a product cost that is hard to see on a spreadsheet but easy to feel in user retention. Buying capacity is also the most reversible-feeling option in one sense: it requires no behavioural change from any team, no renegotiation of internal priorities, and no new failure modes. It is a one-line procurement decision.

But that simplicity is deceptive. Capital hardware is the least reversible commitment on the table. Once purchased, GPUs depreciate whether or not we use them, they consume rack space, power, and cooling we would need to provision, and they lock us into a capacity assumption that may be wrong in either direction. If our workload mix shifts — for instance, if the model distillation work succeeds and per-request compute drops by half — we would be carrying idle silicon. If demand accelerates instead, no single purchase will be enough anyway, and we will face this same decision again with less financial headroom.

**The case for utilisation**

Our current fleet runs at roughly 54% average utilisation, but that average hides the real problem: peaks near 95% during business hours and troughs below 20% overnight. The waste is not in total capacity but in the mismatch between when capacity is demanded and when it is idle. This is a scheduling and architecture problem, not a hardware problem, and it is far cheaper to fix. Concretely, the highest-leverage moves are dynamic batching for inference, migrating our nightly training and evaluation runs into the overnight trough, and building a simple internal priority queue so that low-value batch work yields gracefully to interactive traffic. We estimate these changes could lift effective utilisation into the 75–80% range, which is equivalent to roughly a 40% fleet expansion at near-zero capital cost.

There is also an opportunity cost argument that cuts in favour of utilisation work. The engineering time required — we estimate two engineers for six to eight weeks — is real, but it produces durable capability: better scheduling infrastructure, observability into per-workload cost, and the operational muscle to reason about future capacity decisions quantitatively. Buying hardware teaches us nothing. And if we buy now, we remove the pressure to do this work at all, which means we will carry structural inefficiency into every future scaling decision.

**Reliability and risk**

The honest counterweight is that utilisation gains are not free of risk. Running a fleet hotter reduces headroom for failover, and a tightly packed scheduler is a more fragile system: a single misbehaving job can degrade neighbours in ways a loosely loaded fleet would absorb. We would need to pair the utilisation work with better isolation and load-shedding, which extends the timeline. There is also execution risk — our estimate of 75–80% is a projection, not a measurement, and scheduler projects of this kind routinely land at half their promised gains. This is precisely why we recommend securing purchase options now rather than treating this as a binary choice. The cost of a conditional order or a price hold is small; the cost of discovering in Q3 that utilisation work failed and then waiting twelve weeks for hardware delivery is not.

**Recommendation**

Fund the utilisation project immediately with a hard checkpoint at eight weeks. If effective utilisation reaches 70% or better and p95 latency returns under 250ms, defer the purchase one quarter and reassess against actual demand growth. If it does not, execute the pre-negotiated purchase without further debate. Either branch leaves us with better observability and a defensible answer to the question of how much hardware we actually need — which, ultimately, is the question we are being asked to answer.

We are happy to walk through the telemetry in detail at Thursday's review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next eight weeks on utilisation work before committing to any hardware purchase. The evidence suggests that a meaningful share of our capacity problem is self-inflicted, and the cost of finding out is far lower than the cost of buying our way out prematurely. If utilisation work stalls or demand keeps growing faster than we can reclaim capacity, we should then purchase — and we should start procurement paperwork now so that a later decision is not delayed by process.

**Where we stand**

Our four A100 nodes currently run at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, but that number hides a lot. Peak-hour utilisation on two nodes approaches saturation, while the other two sit mostly idle overnight and on weekends. Batch jobs and interactive inference compete for the same resources without a coherent scheduling policy, and our largest models are pinned to specific nodes for reasons that predate the current team. Meanwhile, our latency SLO is breached a few times a week during peak windows, and those breaches are the proximate cause of the pressure to buy more hardware.

**The case for buying**

Buying is simple and fast. Lead times are now reasonable, capital is available in this year's budget, and additional nodes would immediately relieve peak congestion. There is also a genuine reliability argument: with four nodes, losing one to maintenance or failure removes a quarter of our capacity, and our current headroom is thin enough that a single hardware incident can push us into sustained SLO violations. A fifth or sixth node would materially improve fault tolerance, not just throughput. These are real benefits and I do not want to minimise them.

**The case for utilisation first**

The problem is that buying now would lock in a decision based on a distorted picture of our demand. Our utilisation is low enough that even modest improvements — better batching, a proper queue with priority classes, consolidating model replicas, moving batch workloads to off-peak windows — could plausibly absorb several months of demand growth. The engineering effort involved is perhaps four to six weeks of one or two engineers, work that has value regardless of what we later decide. Scheduling and batching improvements carry over to any future fleet; they are not wasted even if we buy hardware next quarter.

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and this is the crux. If we buy now, we spend capital and, more importantly, we spend the *option* of learning whether our constraints were real. Hardware we buy sits on the balance sheet, consumes power and maintenance attention, and is difficult to resell at anything close to cost. If we defer buying and turn out to be wrong, the penalty is a few more weeks of occasional latency breaches — annoying, visible, but recoverable. The asymmetry favours waiting, provided we set a clear trigger for revisiting the decision.

**Reversibility**

This is fundamentally a question of reversibility. Utilisation work is cheap to reverse: if it fails, we have lost time and gained knowledge. A hardware purchase is expensive to reverse: depreciation, resale losses, and the operational burden of a larger fleet persist for years. When one path preserves options and the other forecloses them, and when the evidence for urgency is ambiguous, we should take the reversible path first.

**Reliability, honestly stated**

I want to be careful not to oversell utilisation work as a reliability solution. Better scheduling reduces contention but does not protect us against node failure; only redundancy does. If our availability target requires N+1 capacity at peak, and we are currently below that, then some purchase is likely inevitable. The utilisation work tells us *how much* to buy, not whether the answer is zero. That is still worth doing: the difference between buying two nodes and buying one is real money and real rack space.

**Uncertainty**

Our demand forecast is the weakest input in this analysis. If the growth we saw last quarter was a one-off driven by a single customer pilot, we may not need new hardware for a year. If it reflects a durable trend, the eight-week delay costs us little because procurement lead time is comparable. Either way, the option value of waiting is high.

**Proposed next steps**

We will begin the utilisation work immediately, define explicit latency and utilisation triggers that would activate the purchase path, and prepare procurement documentation in parallel so that a decision to buy, once made, can execute without further delay. We will revisit this in eight weeks with data rather than impressions.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI compute capacity for the next two quarters

**Status and context**

Our inference and fine-tuning workloads have grown faster than anyone forecast six months ago. We are now running our eight A100s at roughly 78% average utilisation, with evening peaks pushing past 95% and occasional queue times that our internal customers have started to notice. Two proposals are on the table. The first is to purchase four additional GPUs, roughly £180k including networking, racks, and the electrical work our facilities team says is unavoidable. The second is to invest two to three engineer-months in scheduling, batching, and model-serving improvements, plus a modest spend on better observability, to raise effective utilisation of the fleet we already own. This memo argues for the second path first, with the purchase decision deferred but not abandoned.

**The cost picture**

The headline price of new hardware is only part of the story. Beyond the capital outlay there is ongoing power and cooling, which our facilities lead estimates at £2,100 per month for the proposed expansion, and the softer but real cost of operational attention: more machines mean more failure domains, more driver and firmware maintenance, and more capacity planning overhead. Against that, the utilisation work is almost entirely labour we already pay for. If we lift average utilisation from 78% to 90%, we effectively add the equivalent of one and a half GPUs of throughput for the cost of a quarter of an engineer-year. The economics are not close at current scale. The purchase only becomes clearly attractive if demand keeps compounding and we genuinely cannot squeeze more from the existing fleet.

**Latency and user experience**

This is where the utilisation argument needs honesty. Higher utilisation is not free. Queueing behaviour is nonlinear: as a cluster approaches saturation, tail latency degrades sharply, and our interactive inference endpoints are sensitive to p99 latency in a way batch jobs are not. Naively packing more work onto the same machines would trade throughput for user-visible sluggishness, which is a bad trade for the product teams relying on us. The right framing is therefore not "raise utilisation everywhere" but "separate workloads and schedule them intelligently." Batch fine-tuning and offline evaluation can tolerate deep queues and should be allowed to fill idle capacity, while interactive traffic gets reserved headroom. Done properly, this raises fleet-wide utilisation without touching interactive p99s. Done carelessly, it makes everything worse. The engineering discipline required is real, and we should not pretend otherwise.

**Reliability and risk**

There is a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy: a single node failure today takes out 12.5% of our capacity, and the same failure in a twelve-GPU fleet would take out 8%. That is a genuine benefit of expansion. But the utilisation path also improves reliability in a subtler way, because better scheduling gives us the ability to drain and restart nodes for maintenance without dropping work, and better observability means we catch thermal and memory issues before they become hard failures. On balance I judge the reliability gains from the software work to be comparable to those from the hardware, with the caveat that we remain exposed to correlated failures, such as a rack-level power event, that only physical diversity would mitigate.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The strongest argument for deferring the purchase is optionality. GPU prices and availability have been volatile, and there is a reasonable chance that next-generation hardware at better price-performance will be available within our decision window. Money spent now on machines that are merely adequate locks us in; money spent on scheduling and serving software is portable, since it benefits any future fleet regardless of vendor. Conversely, the utilisation work has its own opportunity cost: those are engineer-months not spent on product features, and if the work stalls or underdelivers, we will have delayed capacity relief by a quarter. That is the main downside risk of this recommendation, and it is why we should timebox the effort and define, in advance, the utilisation and latency thresholds that would trigger the purchase regardless.

**Recommendation**

Fund the utilisation programme now, with a hard review at the end of the quarter. If average utilisation exceeds 88% with interactive p99s holding steady, or if the work fails to reach 85% for reasons we understand, proceed with the hardware purchase immediately. I estimate a 60–70% chance this path avoids the purchase entirely for two quarters, but I want to be clear that this is a judgement call under real uncertainty about demand growth, not a certainty. The worst outcome is not choosing wrong; it is choosing slowly. Let's decide at the review, whichever way the data points.

**To:** Engineering Leadership

**Re:** Recommendation on our compute capacity decision for the next two quarters

The case for buying is straightforward on its face. Our p99 latency has crept from 180ms to 340ms over the past three months, and we've had two incidents where queue depth caused timeouts during peak hours. Every additional node we buy is a known quantity: it slots into our existing orchestration, it's provisioned in a day, and the latency problem goes away immediately. The capital cost, roughly $180K for a comparable node, is painful but not existential, and the finance team has confirmed budget is available this quarter but likely not the next.

But the utilization numbers tell a more interesting story. Our fleet-wide average GPU utilization sits at 41%, and even at peak we rarely exceed 65%. The problem isn't raw capacity; it's that our batch scheduler was built for a workload profile we no longer have. Jobs are pinned to specific nodes, small requests monopolize large cards, and our autoscaling reacts to load with a fifteen-minute lag, which means we over-provision for spikes we can predict and under-provision for the ones we can't. If we fixed scheduling alone, I'd estimate we recover 25–30% of effective capacity. That's most of a node's worth of compute, sitting idle because of software we wrote ourselves and can change.

The opportunity cost cuts both ways, and this is where I keep going back and forth. Every engineering week we spend on scheduler improvements is a week not spent on the model quality work that actually drives revenue. The team has maybe six engineer-weeks of genuine bandwidth for infrastructure this quarter. A scheduler rewrite that recovers capacity is valuable, but it's also a project with a history of scope creep, and if it slips, we end up having spent the quarter neither fixing the problem nor buying our way out of it. Buying hardware, by contrast, costs money but almost no attention — and attention, right now, is our scarcer resource.

Reliability is the factor that tips me, though. Right now we have no redundancy: a single node failure takes 50% of our serving capacity offline, and our last hardware incident cost us four hours of degraded service. A second node doesn't just add capacity; it halves our blast radius and lets us do maintenance without scheduling around traffic valleys. Software improvements, however elegant, do nothing for our single-point-of-failure problem. Utilization gains and resilience gains are different currencies, and we're currently poor in only one of them.

There's also the question of reversibility, and hardware looks worse here than it did a year ago. GPU resale values have softened as the rental market matures, and the generation we'd buy today will likely be worth meaningfully less in eighteen months. Scheduler work, by contrast, is an investment in code we keep regardless of how our workload evolves. If our traffic doubles, both paths serve us; if our traffic plateaus or shifts to a different model architecture with different serving characteristics, the scheduler work survives and the hardware may not.

So my recommendation is a split, weighted toward software: fund the scheduler and batching improvements now, with a hard scope and a six-week deadline, and treat the hardware purchase as a pre-authorized fallback rather than a parallel track. If utilization doesn't reach 55% fleet-wide, or if p99 latency hasn't returned under 250ms by the end of that window, we buy the node without further debate. This sequencing costs us six weeks of latency pain we could have avoided, and I want to be honest that this is the price of the option. If leadership judges that six weeks of degraded p99 is unacceptable — and there's a reasonable argument that it is, given our enterprise SLAs — then we should buy now and do the scheduler work anyway, because the utilization problem doesn't disappear with more hardware; it just gets more expensive to ignore.

The genuine uncertainty here is demand. Our traffic forecast has a wide error band, and the growth curve that justifies buying is the same one that makes the scheduler investment pay off fastest. I'd rather make the reversible bet first and keep the irreversible one in our pocket.
